content.introduction: Three academic passages covering Environment and Ecology. 60 minutes, 40 questions.

parts.title: Passage 1: Climate Change and Coral Reefs
parts.text:
Rising ocean temperatures are bleaching coral reefs at an unprecedented rate. Scientists estimate that more than half of the Great Barrier Reef experienced bleaching events in 2016 and 2017 alone. Coral bleaching occurs when water warms by even one degree Celsius above the seasonal average, causing corals to expel the symbiotic algae that provide their colour and up to 90 percent of their energy. Without the algae, corals turn white and become vulnerable to disease.

The ecological consequences extend beyond the reefs themselves. Coral ecosystems support an estimated 25 percent of all marine species despite covering less than one percent of the ocean floor. Fish populations, crustaceans, and invertebrates that depend on reef structures for shelter and breeding are all at risk. Fishing communities across Southeast Asia, the Caribbean, and the Pacific Islands report declining catches as reef degradation reduces the carrying capacity of coastal fisheries.

Restoration efforts are underway in several regions. Marine biologists in Florida and Australia have established coral nurseries, growing heat-tolerant coral fragments on underwater frames before transplanting them to damaged reefs. Genetic research aims to accelerate the selective breeding of naturally resilient coral strains. Critics argue that restoration alone cannot address reefs at the scale required and that only aggressive reductions in greenhouse gas emissions can prevent further loss.
tips: TRUE/FALSE: answer only from the text, not from background knowledge.
Scan for key nouns from each question before reading paragraph by paragraph.
NOT GIVEN: the passage neither confirms nor denies — resist assumptions.

questions.prompt: Coral bleaching occurs when water temperature drops significantly.
questions.answerLine: Bleaching occurs when water warms by even one degree above the seasonal average.

questions.prompt: Coral reefs support approximately 25 percent of all marine species.
questions.answerLine: Coral ecosystems support an estimated 25 percent of all marine species.

questions.prompt: The passage states that restoration alone is sufficient to save all reefs.
questions.answerLine: Critics argue restoration alone cannot address reefs at the scale required.

questions.prompt: What do the symbiotic algae provide to coral?
options: B. Up to 90 percent of their energy
questions.answerLine: Algae provide their colour and up to 90 percent of their energy.

questions.prompt: Scientists grow heat-tolerant coral fragments in underwater ___.
questions.answerLine: Established coral nurseries, growing heat-tolerant coral fragments on underwater frames.

parts.title: Passage 2: Urban Green Spaces and Mental Health
parts.text:
Research over the past two decades has established a consistent association between access to urban green spaces and improved mental health outcomes. Studies conducted in the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and Japan report that residents living within 300 metres of a park or green corridor experience lower rates of anxiety, depression, and stress-related illness. The proposed mechanisms include opportunities for physical activity, social interaction, and what psychologists call restorative attention — the effortless, involuntary engagement that natural environments elicit, allowing deliberate attention networks to recover.

Urban planners have begun incorporating these findings into city design frameworks. Several European cities have adopted green infrastructure standards requiring a minimum ratio of green space per resident. Singapore's 'City in a Garden' strategy has integrated trees and vegetation into public transport hubs, commercial buildings, and residential towers. Landscape architects now speak of biophilic design — the intentional embedding of natural elements into built environments to reconnect urban residents with nature.

Equity concerns complicate the policy picture. Green spaces are not distributed equally across urban areas. In many cities, wealthier neighbourhoods have more parks, tree canopy cover, and maintained recreational areas than lower-income districts. Research in the United States found a strong correlation between median household income and nearby park quality, raising questions about whether urban greening policies reinforce or address existing inequalities.
tips: Match headings to paragraph topics, not isolated details.
MCQ: identify what the question asks before reading options.
Fill-in-blank: the exact word(s) from the passage are usually correct.

questions.prompt: Access to green spaces within 300 metres is linked to lower anxiety rates.
questions.answerLine: Residents living within 300 metres of a park experience lower rates of anxiety.

questions.prompt: The involuntary engagement with nature is called ___ attention.
questions.answerLine: What psychologists call restorative attention.

questions.prompt: What does 'biophilic design' mean?
options: B. Embedding natural elements into built environments
C. Using solar panels on buildings
questions.answerLine: Biophilic design — the intentional embedding of natural elements into built environments.

parts.title: Passage 3: Rewilding: Restoring Lost Ecosystems
parts.text:
Rewilding is a conservation strategy that aims to restore natural processes and, in some cases, reintroduce species that have been locally or regionally extinct for decades or centuries. Unlike traditional conservation, which often focuses on maintaining landscapes in a fixed historical state, rewilding emphasises dynamic ecological processes — predation, competition, and disturbance — as drivers of biodiversity.

The reintroduction of wolves to Yellowstone National Park in 1995 is frequently cited as a landmark rewilding experiment. Wolves reduced overgrazing by elk, allowing riparian vegetation to recover along riverbanks. The restored plant cover stabilised stream banks, altered water flow patterns, and created new habitat for beavers, songbirds, and fish. Ecologists describe this chain of interactions as a trophic cascade — a series of ecosystem effects triggered by changes at the top of the food chain.

European rewilding projects have focused on reintroducing beavers, lynx, and bison to areas where they were once native. The return of beavers to Scotland has been linked to improved water quality and flood moderation downstream. However, rewilding also generates conflict. Farmers and land managers raise concerns about livestock predation and loss of agricultural land. Ecologists counter that compensatory mechanisms, habitat buffers, and careful monitoring can manage such risks, though tensions between conservation goals and rural livelihoods remain an ongoing challenge.
tips: Passage 3 is the most difficult — allocate 25 minutes.
Track argument structure: claim → evidence → counter-claim.
Do not bring in external knowledge — answer from the text only.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between rewilding and traditional conservation?
options: A. Rewilding focuses on dynamic ecological processes rather than fixed states
B. Traditional conservation allows more predation
C. Rewilding only applies to marine environments
questions.answerLine: Rewilding emphasises dynamic ecological processes rather than maintaining landscapes in a fixed state.

questions.prompt: The wolf reintroduction in Yellowstone reduced overgrazing by elk.
questions.answerLine: Wolves reduced overgrazing by elk, allowing riparian vegetation to recover.

questions.prompt: A ___ cascade describes ecosystem effects triggered by changes at the top of the food chain.
questions.answerLine: Ecologists describe this chain of interactions as a trophic cascade.

questions.prompt: All farmers support rewilding projects in Europe.
questions.answerLine: The passage mentions conflict but does not say all farmers oppose it.

questions.prompt: Beaver reintroduction in Scotland has been linked to
options: B. Improved water quality and flood moderation
C. Destruction of local fish populations
questions.answerLine: Linked to improved water quality and flood moderation downstream.

parts.title: Passage 1: Vaccine Hesitancy and Public Health
parts.text:
Research into vaccine hesitancy and public health has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in environment and ecology. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in environment and ecology have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.

Scan for key nouns from each question before reading paragraph by paragraph.
NOT GIVEN: the passage neither confirms nor denies — resist assumptions.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Mental Health
parts.text:
The Impact of Mental Health represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary environment and ecology research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in environment and ecology are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. parts.title: Passage 1: Vaccine Hesitancy and Public Health
parts.text:
Vaccine Hesitancy and Public Health represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary environment and ecology research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in environment and ecology are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.
tips: TRUE/FALSE: answer only from the text, not from background knowledge.
Scan for key nouns from each question before reading paragraph by paragraph.
NOT GIVEN: the passage neither confirms nor denies — resist assumptions.

parts.title: Passage 1: Vaccine Hesitancy and Public Health
parts.text:
Research into vaccine hesitancy and public health has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in environment and ecology. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in environment and ecology have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Mental Health
parts.text:
The Impact of Mental Health represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary environment and ecology research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in environment and ecology are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.

parts.title: Passage 1: The Rise of Quantum Computing
parts.text:
Quantum computing promises to solve computational problems that would take classical computers millions of years to process. Unlike classical computers, which encode information as binary bits — either 0 or 1 — quantum computers use qubits, which can exist in multiple states simultaneously through a property called superposition. A second quantum property, entanglement, allows qubits to be correlated in ways that enable massively parallel processing.

The potential applications are far-reaching. Pharmaceutical companies are exploring quantum simulation to model molecular interactions at an atomic level, potentially accelerating drug discovery by years. Cryptographers note a more troubling implication: a sufficiently powerful quantum computer could break the RSA encryption underpinning most of today's internet security. Governments and technology companies are investing heavily in post-quantum cryptography to develop encryption methods resistant to quantum attack.

Practical quantum computers remain technically immature. Qubits are extremely sensitive to environmental disturbance, a phenomenon called decoherence, which introduces errors into calculations. Error correction requires large numbers of physical qubits to maintain a single reliable logical qubit, placing enormous demands on hardware. Current machines operate with tens to hundreds of qubits; industry experts estimate that fault-tolerant general-purpose quantum computers may require millions of stable qubits.
tips: TRUE/FALSE: answer only from the text, not from background knowledge.
Scan for key nouns from each question before reading paragraph by paragraph.
NOT GIVEN: the passage neither confirms nor denies — resist assumptions.

questions.answerLine: Classical computers encode information as binary bits — 0 or 1.

questions.answerLine: Multiple states simultaneously through a property called superposition.

questions.prompt: Why are governments investing in post-quantum cryptography?
options: A. To speed up classical computers
B. To develop encryption resistant to quantum attacks
C. To replace all existing computers
questions.answerLine: Develop encryption methods resistant to quantum attack.

questions.prompt: Environmental disturbance that introduces errors is called ___.
questions.answerLine: A phenomenon called decoherence, which introduces errors into calculations.

parts.title: Passage 2: Artificial Intelligence and Creative Industries
parts.text:
The integration of artificial intelligence into creative industries has generated debate about authorship, originality, and the economic future of human artists. AI systems trained on vast datasets of existing artwork, music, and text can now generate content that is, in many cases, indistinguishable from human-produced work to the untrained eye. The commercial applications are broad: advertising agencies use AI-generated imagery, music streaming services employ algorithmic composition for ambient tracks, and publishers experiment with AI-assisted editorial and writing tools.

Creative professionals have responded with a mixture of concern and adaptation. Visual artists raise the question of consent, arguing that training AI systems on copyrighted works without permission or compensation constitutes appropriation of intellectual labour. Legal systems in multiple jurisdictions are grappling with whether AI-generated content can be copyrighted and, if so, who holds the copyright — the AI developer, the user who prompted the output, or no one. Court decisions in the United States have so far declined to extend copyright protection to works with no human author.

Others argue that the history of creative tools is a history of disruption: photography did not destroy painting; digital audio workstations transformed rather than eliminated professional music production. They contend that AI will become one more instrument in the human creative toolkit, augmenting rather than replacing artistic expression, particularly in areas requiring emotional depth, cultural context, and lived experience.

parts.title: Passage 3: Autonomous Vehicles: Progress and Barriers
parts.text:
Autonomous vehicles (AVs) have attracted hundreds of billions of dollars in investment from established automakers, technology companies, and specialist startups. The promise is transformative: self-driving cars could reduce road accidents caused by human error, which account for over 90 percent of all collisions. Mobility services for elderly and disabled populations could be democratised. Freight logistics could be streamlined by trucks that operate around the clock without driver fatigue constraints.

Technical progress has been significant but uneven. Leading AV developers report that their systems perform reliably in clear weather on well-mapped highway routes. Urban environments present greater challenges: unpredictable pedestrian behaviour, construction zones, poor lane markings, and adverse weather all degrade sensor accuracy. The AI systems guiding AVs must make split-second decisions in edge cases — scenarios they have not been specifically trained for — raising questions about safety thresholds and liability when accidents occur.

Regulatory frameworks are evolving slowly. Most jurisdictions currently require a human driver to remain alert and able to take control at all times in Level 3 autonomous vehicles, undermining one of the main consumer benefits. Fully autonomous Level 5 vehicles remain limited to controlled testing environments in a small number of cities globally. Consumer trust remains low: surveys consistently show that most people would feel uncomfortable as a passenger in a fully autonomous vehicle, even if the technology were certified as statistically safer than human driving.

parts.title: Passage 1: The Science of Sleep
parts.text:
The Science of Sleep represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary technology and innovation research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in technology and innovation are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Memory Consolidation
parts.text:
Research into the impact of memory consolidation has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in technology and innovation. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in technology and innovation have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.

parts.title: Passage 1: The Science of Sleep
parts.text:
Research into the science of sleep has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in technology and innovation. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in technology and innovation have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Memory Consolidation
parts.text:
The Impact of Memory Consolidation represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary technology and innovation research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in technology and innovation are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.

The bar chart below shows the levels of participation in education and the employment rate for women in Edinburgh in 2008.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

parts.title: Task 2: Essay - Government Support for Elderly People

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Urban Sensors
parts.text:
Research into the impact of urban sensors has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in health and medicine. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in health and medicine have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.
tips: Match headings to paragraph topics, not isolated details.
MCQ: identify what the question asks before reading options.
Fill-in-blank: the exact word(s) from the passage are usually correct.

parts.title: Passage 1: Smart Cities and Data
parts.text:
Research into smart cities and data has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in health and medicine. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in health and medicine have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.

NOT GIVEN: the passage neither confirms nor denies — resist assumptions.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Urban Sensors
parts.text:
The Impact of Urban Sensors represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary health and medicine research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in health and medicine are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.

The graph below shows the population change between 1940 and 2000 in three different parts of the world.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

parts.title: Task 2: Essay - Factors Influencing News Editorial Decisions
parts.text:
News editors decide what to broadcast on television and what to print in newspapers. What factors do you think influence these decisions?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

parts.title: Passage 1: Smart Cities and Data
parts.text:
Research into smart cities and data has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in health and medicine. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in health and medicine have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.
tips: TRUE/FALSE: answer only from the text, not from background knowledge.
Scan for key nouns from each question before reading paragraph by paragraph.
NOT GIVEN: the passage neither confirms nor denies — resist assumptions.

parts.title: Passage 1: Microfinance and Poverty
parts.text:
Research into microfinance and poverty has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in education and learning. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in education and learning have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.

Scan for key nouns from each question before reading paragraph by paragraph.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Small Loans
parts.text:
The Impact of Small Loans represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary education and learning research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in education and learning are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.

The charts below show the changes in ownership of electrical appliances and amount of time spent doing housework in households in one country between 1920 and 2019.

tips: Begin with an overview of the most striking trend or feature.

Use precise comparative language: 'rose sharply', 'remained relatively stable', 'fell significantly'.

parts.title: Task 2: Essay - University Education for All

University education should be available to all students, regardless of their financial situation.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
tips: Clearly state your position in the introduction.
Each body paragraph should have one main idea + evidence + explanation.
Conclude by restating your view — do not introduce new ideas.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Small Loans

International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.

parts.title: Passage 1: Microfinance and Poverty
parts.text:
Microfinance and Poverty represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary education and learning research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in education and learning are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Small Loans
parts.text:
Research into the impact of small loans has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in education and learning. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in education and learning have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Online Platforms
parts.text:
Research into the impact of online platforms has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in urban planning and architecture. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in urban planning and architecture have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.

parts.title: Passage 3: Newspaper Industry Decline
parts.text:

Social dimensions add further complexity. parts.title: Passage 1: Censorship in the Digital Age
parts.text:
Censorship in the Digital Age represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary urban planning and architecture research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in urban planning and architecture are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Online Platforms
parts.text:
Research into the impact of online platforms has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in urban planning and architecture. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in urban planning and architecture have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.

content.title: Cambridge 5 Test 4 - Writing
content.introduction: Task 1: minimum 150 words, 20 minutes. Task 2: minimum 250 words, 40 minutes.

parts.title: Task 1: Bar Chart - Education Qualifications in Europe 2002
parts.text:
The bar chart below shows the percentage of students who gained a qualification at different levels of education in three European countries in 2002.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.
tips: Begin with an overview of the most striking trend or feature.
Group related data — do not describe every single figure.
Use precise comparative language: 'rose sharply', 'remained relatively stable', 'fell significantly'.

questions.prompt:
The bar chart below shows the percentage of students who gained a qualification at different levels of education in three European countries in 2002.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.
questions.answerLine: Identify the key trend before writing.

questions.prompt: Overview check: What comparison is most relevant?
questions.answerLine: State the most important comparison in your overview paragraph.

parts.title: Task 2: Essay - Advantages and Disadvantages of Telecommuting
parts.text:
"Telecommuting" refers to workers doing their jobs from home for part of each week and communicating with their office using computer technology. Telecommuting is growing in many countries and is having an impact on the environment and on society.

Discuss the possible advantages and disadvantages of telecommuting.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
tips: Clearly state your position in the introduction.
Each body paragraph should have one main idea + evidence + explanation.
Conclude by restating your view — do not introduce new ideas.

content.title: Cambridge 5 Test 4 - Speaking
content.introduction: Speaking test: Part 1 (4-5 min), Part 2 (3-4 min), Part 3 (4-5 min). Speak naturally and extend each answer.

parts.title: Part 1: Interview
parts.text: The examiner will ask about familiar topics: neighbourhood, transport, shopping. Give natural answers of 2-4 sentences each.
tips: Do not memorise scripts — speak naturally and conversationally.
Add one reason or example to each answer.
Avoid one-word responses.

questions.prompt: Where are you from?
Do you work or study?
What do you enjoy doing in your free time?
What are the most popular activities in your country?

parts.title: Part 2: Individual Long Turn
parts.text:
Describe something important to you from your home country.

You should say:
  what it is
  where it comes from
  how it is used
and explain why it is important.
tips: Use your 1 minute to note 4-5 key words or phrases.
Speak continuously for up to 2 minutes — do not stop early.
End with the 'why' section — it carries significant marks.

questions.prompt:
Describe something important to you from your home country.

You should say:
  what it is
  where it comes from
  how it is used
and explain why it is important.

parts.title: Part 3: Discussion
parts.text: Broader questions about urban development, housing. Develop each answer with an idea, reason, and example or prediction.
tips: Show range with phrases like: 'It depends on...', 'From a different perspective...'
Use hedging language: 'I would argue that...', 'It seems to me that...'
Compare across time, cultures, or social groups where relevant.

questions.prompt: How important is your cultural heritage to you?
Do younger generations value their cultural traditions?
How can traditions be preserved in modern society?
What role does the government play in preserving culture?
Is it important for countries to have a strong national identity?
How has globalisation affected local cultures?

parts.title: Section 1: Festival Volunteer Registration

parts.title: Task 1: Pie Charts - Electricity Production by Fuel Source
parts.text:
The pie charts below show units of electricity production by fuel source in Australia and France in 1980 and 2000.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.
tips: Begin with an overview of the most striking trend or feature.
Group related data — do not describe every single figure.
Use precise comparative language: 'rose sharply', 'remained relatively stable', 'fell significantly'.

parts.title: Task 2: Essay - Destruction of World Forests
parts.text:
Forests are the lungs of the earth. Destruction of the world's forests amounts to death of the world we currently know. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
tips: Clearly state your position in the introduction.
Each body paragraph should have one main idea + evidence + explanation.
Conclude by restating your view — do not introduce new ideas.

parts.title: Passage 1: Underwater Archaeology
parts.text:
Underwater Archaeology represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary business and economics research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in business and economics are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.
tips: TRUE/FALSE: answer only from the text, not from background knowledge.
Scan for key nouns from each question before reading paragraph by paragraph.
NOT GIVEN: the passage neither confirms nor denies — resist assumptions.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Shipwrecks
parts.text:
Research into the impact of shipwrecks has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in business and economics. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in business and economics have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.
tips: Match headings to paragraph topics, not isolated details.
MCQ: identify what the question asks before reading options.
Fill-in-blank: the exact word(s) from the passage are usually correct.

parts.title: Passage 1: Underwater Archaeology
parts.text:
Research into underwater archaeology has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in business and economics. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in business and economics have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.

content.title: Cambridge 6 Test 3 - Writing
content.introduction: Task 1: minimum 150 words, 20 minutes. Task 2: minimum 250 words, 40 minutes.

parts.title: Task 1: Charts - Fast Food Spending in UK
parts.text:
The bar chart below shows the amount of money per week spent on fast foods in the UK, and the graphs show the trends in consumption of fast foods.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.
tips: Begin with an overview of the most striking trend or feature.
Group related data — do not describe every single figure.
Use precise comparative language: 'rose sharply', 'remained relatively stable', 'fell significantly'.

questions.prompt:

Write at least 150 words.
questions.answerLine: Identify the key trend before writing.

questions.prompt: Overview check: What comparison is most relevant?
questions.answerLine: State the most important comparison in your overview paragraph.

parts.title: Task 2: Essay - Reducing Poverty: Growth vs Aid
parts.text:
The best way to reduce poverty in developing countries is through economic growth rather than increasing aid. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
tips: Clearly state your position in the introduction.
Each body paragraph should have one main idea + evidence + explanation.
Conclude by restating your view — do not introduce new ideas.

content.title: Cambridge 6 Test 3 - Speaking
content.introduction: Speaking test: Part 1 (4-5 min), Part 2 (3-4 min), Part 3 (4-5 min). Speak naturally and extend each answer.

parts.title: Part 1: Interview
parts.text: The examiner will ask about familiar topics: money, work, leisure. Give natural answers of 2-4 sentences each.
tips: Do not memorise scripts — speak naturally and conversationally.
Add one reason or example to each answer.
Avoid one-word responses.

questions.prompt: Where are you from?
Do you work or study?
What do you enjoy doing in your free time?
What are the most popular activities in your country?

parts.title: Part 2: Individual Long Turn
parts.text:
Describe something important to you from your home country.

You should say:
  what it is
  where it comes from
  how it is used
and explain why it is important.
tips: Use your 1 minute to note 4-5 key words or phrases.
Speak continuously for up to 2 minutes — do not stop early.
End with the 'why' section — it carries significant marks.

questions.prompt:

You should say:
  what it is
  where it comes from
  how it is used
and explain why it is important.

parts.title: Part 3: Discussion
parts.text: Broader questions about work-life balance, entrepreneurship. Develop each answer with an idea, reason, and example or prediction.
tips: Show range with phrases like: 'It depends on...', 'From a different perspective...'
Use hedging language: 'I would argue that...', 'It seems to me that...'
Compare across time, cultures, or social groups where relevant.

questions.prompt: How important is your cultural heritage to you?
Do younger generations value their cultural traditions?
How can traditions be preserved in modern society?

parts.title: Passage 1: The Psychology of Procrastination
parts.text:
The Psychology of Procrastination represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary arts and culture research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in arts and culture are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.
tips: TRUE/FALSE: answer only from the text, not from background knowledge.
Scan for key nouns from each question before reading paragraph by paragraph.
NOT GIVEN: the passage neither confirms nor denies — resist assumptions.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Motivation
parts.text:
Research into the impact of motivation has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in arts and culture. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in arts and culture have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.
tips: Match headings to paragraph topics, not isolated details.
MCQ: identify what the question asks before reading options.
Fill-in-blank: the exact word(s) from the passage are usually correct.

parts.title: Passage 1: The Psychology of Procrastination
parts.text:
Research into the psychology of procrastination has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in arts and culture. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in arts and culture have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Motivation
parts.text:
The Impact of Motivation represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary arts and culture research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in arts and culture are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.

parts.title: Task 1: Process Diagram - How Coffee is Produced

The diagram below shows how coffee is produced and prepared for sale.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.
tips: Begin with an overview of the most striking trend or feature.
Group related data — do not describe every single figure.
Use precise comparative language: 'rose sharply', 'remained relatively stable', 'fell significantly'.

parts.title: Task 2: Essay - Single-sex vs Mixed Schools
parts.text:
Some people think that it is better to educate boys and girls in separate schools. Others, however, believe that boys and girls benefit more from attending mixed schools.

Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
tips: Clearly state your position in the introduction.
Each body paragraph should have one main idea + evidence + explanation.
Conclude by restating your view — do not introduce new ideas.

content.title: Cambridge 7 Test 2 - Speaking
content.introduction: Speaking test: Part 1 (4-5 min), Part 2 (3-4 min), Part 3 (4-5 min). Speak naturally and extend each answer.

parts.title: Part 1: Interview
parts.text: The examiner will ask about familiar topics: music, art, films. Give natural answers of 2-4 sentences each.
tips: Do not memorise scripts — speak naturally and conversationally.
Add one reason or example to each answer.
Avoid one-word responses.

Do you play any musical instruments?
Do you think music is important?
Has music changed a lot in your country over the years?

parts.title: Part 2: Individual Long Turn
parts.text:
Describe an advertisement you have seen that you found particularly useful or interesting.

You should say:
  where you saw it
  what it was for
  what it involved
and explain why you found it useful or interesting.
tips: Use your 1 minute to note 4-5 key words or phrases.
Speak continuously for up to 2 minutes — do not stop early.
End with the 'why' section — it carries significant marks.

questions.prompt:

  what it involved
